extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and general readers of American journalism history
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and evaluate the practices, risks, financial models, and political roles of American newspapers in the early 19th century (c.1801-1835), including partisan organs, mercantile papers, news-gathering, legal exposure, and editorial style. Emphasis is on features that determined influence, survival, and independence of papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporter’s duty to protect news source
rubrics_metrics.description: “Thus was established the principle of the reporter’s duty to protect his news source.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Nathaniel Rounsavell (brought before the House in 1812 for refusing to divulge a source) and other journalists arrested for the same purpose; this principle could lead to legal jeopardy but was treated as a professional duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press expression hampered during wartime / regional variation in dissent
rubrics_metrics.description: “Though the expression of press opinion is always hampered in war times, the Federalist opposition to the Second War with England was remarkably outspoken, especially in New England.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courage of opposition varied by locality — in some regions editors were outspoken; in others (where war was popular) opposition was suppressed violently (e.g., Baltimore mob storming a printshop).

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspapers as partisan/administrative organs
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers frequently acted as official or semi-official organs of administrations or parties (e.g., National Intelligencer as 'authoritative spokesman for the executive branch', Washington Globe as government spokesman).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being an administration organ afforded official access and printing fees but could displace neutrality and tie editorial line to political fortunes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government patronage and appointments influence editorial independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors and papers often received federal appointments and public printing (e.g., Globe received ~$50,000/year; Jackson’s appointments to journalists), which could be used to 'suborn' the press.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patronage created financial dependence and could shape editorial positions; lists of appointees were used to criticize such influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical dangers to editors and presses (mobs, assaults, duels)
rubrics_metrics.description: Violent protest against newspaper comment took forms of mobs storming pressrooms, individual assaults, and duels (e.g., the famous Burr–Hamilton duel originating from newspaper paragraph).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors risked property destruction, bodily harm, or death; defensive measures (fortifying houses) and consequences (prison storms, killings) are documented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Libel suits and legal risk as routine constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Libel suits were commonplace and could shut down papers (e.g., Cheetham faced many libel actions; Street’s paper stopped by libel verdicts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent litigation shaped editorial aggression and sometimes ended publications; number of suits served as a metric of editorial recklessness or combativeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: News-gathering practices determine competitive advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: Enterprising news-gathering such as obtaining earliest foreign news from incoming vessels and intensive reportage of markets (Wall Street) gave papers an edge (Journal of Commerce, Courier & Enquirer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investment in news-gathering personnel and methods (e.g., boarding ships) correlated with circulation and influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stenographic reporting and newspapers as official recorders
rubrics_metrics.description: Shorthand reporters (e.g., Gales, Seaton, Smith) compiled the record of congressional proceedings; National Intelligencer’s reports were for years the only record of debates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accurate, timely reporting of government proceedings enhanced a paper’s authority and long-term historical value (precursor to formal Congressional records).

rubrics_metrics.name: Format and space-allocation reflect mission and audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers used specific formats — example: a modest four-page paper with first and last pages for advertising and second page for proceedings/editorials; mercantile dailies often devoted nearly all space to commercial announcements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Layout choices signal target readership (merchants vs. politically engaged readers) and revenue model (advertising-driven vs. editorial-driven).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between mercantile and political newspapers
rubrics_metrics.description: Mercantile papers focused on commerce and advertising (Commercial Advertiser, Mercantile Advertiser), while other papers were explicitly devoted to politics; yet mercantile papers still engaged in politics at times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Categorizing a paper as 'mercantile' or 'political' helps predict content mix, editorial tone, and intended readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial style and tone as defining characteristic
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorials ranged from 'fiery' and 'abusive' to 'mild' and 'sententious' — style defined reputation (e.g., Cheetham’s 'rich fluency and abusiveness', Gales’s 'sententious political philosophy').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tone affected influence, libel exposure, and readership; flamboyant or vitriolic styles could win attention but invite suits and reprisals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial management and ownership models affect survival
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors were often poor financiers; founding often depended on loans or patron donations (Hamilton raised funds for Evening Post), and mismanagement could limit growth despite editorial success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Business skill, advertising revenue, and prudent accounting were as important to a paper's longevity as editorial quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial values shape advertising and content policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Some papers refused certain ads or topics for moral/political reasons (Journal of Commerce did not accept theatre or lottery advertising and opposed slavery and Sabbath-breaking).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial stance could limit ad revenue but reinforce brand identity and political consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors as active political strategists and power-brokers
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors sometimes formed strategy boards or 'kitchen cabinets' for leaders (Blair, Kendall, Rives acted as Jackson’s informal advisers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial influence extended beyond commentary into shaping political action and appointments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circulation and advertising revenue as measures of success
rubrics_metrics.description: Circulation figures and ad income indicated prominence (Courier & Enquirer circulation of 4,000; Evening Post advertising >$10,000/year).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantitative metrics like circulation and ad receipts were used to judge a paper’s reach and financial health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of factual, indexed publication for long-term authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Publications like Niles’ Weekly Register devoted to facts, statistics, speeches, and documents, octavo and indexed, achieved wide reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compilations emphasizing factual records and indexing contributed to lasting usefulness and respectability across partisan divides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social standing and networks amplify editorial influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors’ social hospitality and personal relationships (Smith’s soirees frequented by the President; Seaton long mayor) boosted a paper’s prestige and access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal connections enabled access to contributors, government information, and political patronage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mergers, name changes, and volume resets as survival tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Founders frequently changed paper names, reset volume numbering, merged rival papers, or absorbed old papers to take fresh starts (e.g., Greenleaf’s Argus → American Citizen; multiple Boston papers merged into Daily Advertiser).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consolidation could rescue failing titles, reshape political alignments, and concentrate resources; tracking lineage is important for institutional history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional market determines press density and character
rubrics_metrics.description: New York was the newspaper capital with many dailies and weeklies; Washington was influential for political reporting but not the commercial newspaper center; different cities had distinct press ecologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: City population, commercial activity, and political centrality shape number, type, and competitiveness of newspapers.
